forbiddenKeyColumns.name: email
forbiddenKeyColumns.why: An address is a way to reach somebody, not a name for a row. It changes, it is personal data an erasure has to remove, and every reference taken against it breaks when it does.

forbiddenKeyColumns.name: secret
forbiddenKeyColumns.why: A key that is also a credential cannot be logged, put in a URL or shown in an error, which is most of what an identifier is for.

forbiddenKeyColumns.name: filename
forbiddenKeyColumns.why: A file keeps its identity when it is renamed or moved, so the name cannot be the identity.

forbiddenKeyColumns.name: rename-unstable
forbiddenKeyColumns.why: A name is what a reader calls the row today. Identity has to survive the rename.

forbiddenKeyColumns.name: foreign-identifier
forbiddenKeyColumns.why: Another system's identifier is theirs to reuse, recycle or retire, and a provider swap leaves every row unaddressable.

forbiddenKeyColumns.name: positional
forbiddenKeyColumns.why: A position is true only until something is inserted above it.

sequentialKeys.why: An append-only run transcript read only in order, by the owner of the run it hangs off. The sequence is what puts the events back in order after a reconnect, and no route addresses an event by id.
An append-only step log under one turn, ordered by the sequence and reached only through its turn.
An append-only terminal scrollback ordered by the sequence and reached only through its session.
A platform release audit trail read by operators in order; no reader addresses one event.
A hash-chained break-glass trail where the sequence is part of the chain that verifySupportAccessTrail verifies.
An append-only revision history of one plan, ordered by the sequence and reached only through the plan.

forbiddenKeyExemptions.why: The row is the record that one storage object was replicated, so the object key is the thing being identified rather than a name the object happens to carry. A replica is never renamed; a new key is a new object and a new row.
